title: What you think about often
hookLine: whatever one thinks about often, the mind inclines that way (MN 19)

lines: THE SAME WAY ACROSS THE LAWN.
cards: Walk the same way across a lawn every day for a month, and you'll make a path. Nobody planned it. Nobody poured concrete.
The grass just gave up where your feet kept landing, and now everyone walks that way without thinking.
In MN 19, the Buddha says the mind works like that lawn, and he learned it by watching his own mind before his awakening.

teach.b: MN 19, the Dvedhavitakka, the discourse on two kinds of thought. Before his awakening, the Buddha says, he divided his thoughts into two piles. On one side: thoughts of sense desire, ill will and cruelty.
On the other: thoughts of renunciation, goodwill and non-cruelty. When one from the first pile arose, he noticed it plainly: this leads to my own harm, to others' harm, to both; it obstructs wisdom.
And as he noticed, it faded. Then comes the sentence.

Whatever a monk keeps thinking about and pondering, that becomes the inclination of his mind. Think often of ill will, and the mind leans toward ill will. Think often of goodwill, and it leans toward goodwill.
Then a picture from farm life.

teach.h: THE COWHERD BEFORE AND AFTER HARVEST.
teach.b: In the last month of the rainy season, when the crops are thick, a cowherd has to watch his cows constantly, tapping and checking them with a stick to keep them out of the crops, because he can see the trouble coming if they get in.
But in the last month of the hot season, with the harvest in, he can sit at the foot of a tree, or out in the open, and only needs to remember: there are the cows. At first the work is watchful.
Later, the mind leans the right way on its own, and you can rest. The Dhammapada opens on the same ground, in Max Müller's translation: “All that we are is the result of what we have thought.”

how: Buddhist practitioners cultivate wholesome thoughts deliberately, for example through loving-kindness practice or recollecting the qualities of the Buddha, on the understanding that repeated thoughts shape the mind.

o: a fear of speaking in front of others
a silent mantra repeated in meditation
thought: what the mind keeps returning to

p: the cowherd watches with a stick

s: MN 19 describes the Buddha's own thinking before his awakening
he sorted his thoughts into two piles.
the sutta says thoughts pass without shaping the mind
whatever one thinks about often becomes the mind's inclination.
after the harvest, the cowherd still has to watch every step
he can sit under a tree and simply remember: there are the cows.

games.q: the crops are harvested and the fields are bare. what does the cowherd in MN 19 need to do?
o: sit under a tree and just remember: there are the cows
games.why: with no crops at risk, mindfulness is enough. the Buddha uses it for a mind that already leans toward the good.

practice: Choose one good thing to think about on purpose, a person you're grateful for, a kindness someone showed you, a place that calms you, and let it fill the sit. When the mind wanders, and it will, walk it back without scolding.
One more step on the same spot of lawn.

wordCard.voice: Vitakka, thought. Whatever the mind keeps returning to, it starts to lean toward.

orig.note: Pali vitakka: thought, thinking; MN 19 is the dvedhā-vitakka, thoughts split in two.

carryVoice: Your line: the mind inclines. A path across the lawn is made one step at a time. Day four hundred fourteen, done.

sources.q: All that we are is the result of what we have thought
